wine.name: Pétrus
wine.grapes: Merlot, effectively the whole blend; older vintages could carry a small share of Cabernet Franc.
wine.sites: One vineyard at the high point of the Pomerol plateau, on a buttonhole of dense blue clay, a swelling smectite, over the iron rich subsoil the growers call crasse de fer.
wine.making: The grapes are picked in the afternoons, once the dew has dried, by a team large enough to bring in a plot in a few hours. The wine is fermented in concrete vats, aged for about a year and a half in oak barrels, a part of them new, and bottled at the estate.
wine.glass: Black plum, black cherry and truffle over cocoa and a note of iron, with liquorice and violet; dense and velvety, with ripe, fine tannin and a long, warm, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Supple enough to taste young, it then closes and needs fifteen to twenty years in a strong vintage; the great years last half a century.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two and an old one gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The estate's name alone, with no Château before it, under a portrait of Saint Peter holding the keys.
The appellation of the clay and gravel plateau beside Libourne, which has never been classified.

records.table: Almost pure Merlot from a buttonhole of blue clay at the top of the Pomerol plateau, Pétrus carries no classification at all. It is plum, truffle and velvet, and needs years in bottle before it opens.
records.story: At the Universal Exhibition in Paris in 1878 a Pomerol wine won a gold medal, an early sign of fame for a commune the brokers of 1855 had passed over: Pétrus, then the property of the Arnaud family, named for Saint Peter, whose portrait with the keys of heaven appears on every label. From 1925 Madame Edmonde Loubat, who kept a hotel in Libourne and died in 1961, bought into the estate, and over the next two decades she gathered it into her own hands. After the Second World War she gave the young Libourne merchant Jean-Pierre Moueix (1913 to 2003) the sole right to sell the wine, and the 1947 that followed is a vintage of history. When the frost of February 1956 killed vines across the Right Bank, the estate cut its vines back to the stock rather than pull them up, as the story is told, and so kept their age. After Madame Loubat's death the Moueix family bought a share from her heirs, and in 1969 a parcel of neighbouring Château Gazin joined the vineyard. Pomerol never drew up a ranking, and Pétrus has never needed one: its standing rests on the clay, the Merlot and the care of one family of merchants.

others.name: La Fleur-Pétrus
others.note: A separate estate on the Pomerol plateau, long run by the Moueix house of Libourne; a different wine, not a second wine of Pétrus.

traps: Pétrus holds no classification: Pomerol has never been ranked, so a list that calls it a first growth is wrong.
The label reads Pétrus alone; there is no Château before the name.
Pétrus makes no second wine: La Fleur-Pétrus and Trotanoy are separate Pomerol estates, not lesser bottlings of it.

cards.front: Pétrus: what is the soil under its vineyard, and why does it matter?
cards.back: A buttonhole of dense blue clay at the top of the Pomerol plateau, a swelling smectite that rations water to the vines through a dry summer.

cards.front: Which Libourne merchant gained the sole right to sell Pétrus after the Second World War?
cards.back: Jean-Pierre Moueix, whose family bought a share of the estate from the heirs of Madame Loubat after her death in 1961.

questions.q: A guest asks which grape makes Pétrus. Which answer fits?
opts: Cabernet Franc and Merlot in near equal parts
Cabernet Sauvignon first, with Merlot behind
About a third each of three grapes
questions.exp: Pétrus is effectively all Merlot from blue clay; near equal Cabernet Franc and Merlot is Cheval Blanc, and a third each of three grapes is Figeac.

questions.q: From 1925 a Libourne hotel keeper bought into Pétrus and over two decades gathered the estate into her own hands. Who was she?
questions.exp: Madame Loubat bought her first shares in 1925 and held Pétrus until her death in 1961; the other three ran Champagne houses.

wine.name: Le Pin
wine.grapes: Merlot, all or nearly all of it, with a trace of Cabernet Franc in some years.
wine.sites: A small vineyard of gravel over clay on the Pomerol plateau, beside Vieux Château Certan, around the modest house where a lone pine gave the estate its name.
wine.making: Fermented in small vats, the wine is run into new oak barrels for its malolactic fermentation and stays in them for well over a year, which gives the mocha and cream of its style, before it is bottled at the estate.
wine.glass: Ripe plum, black cherry and mocha over cream, vanilla and a little truffle; plush and round, with soft, sweet tannin, gentle acidity and a long, rich finish.
wine.ageing: Open and generous within a few years of the vintage, it keeps its charm for twenty years and more in a strong year.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one only to take it off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The estate's name, from a lone pine tree beside the house; no Château is printed before it.
The appellation of the plateau north east of Libourne, which has no classification of any kind.

records.table: Begun by a Belgian family in 1979, Le Pin is Pomerol Merlot from a few rows of gravel and clay, raised in new oak. Plush and openly ripe, with plum, mocha and cream, it charms far younger than its neighbours.
records.story: A single pine tree beside a modest house gave Le Pin its name. The Thienpont family, wine merchants from Belgium, had owned Vieux Château Certan on the Pomerol plateau since 1924, and in 1979 a branch of the family bought this small plot nearby and named the new estate after the tree. The first vintage was made that same autumn, and from the start the wine went into new oak barrels, where it also finished its malolactic fermentation. The early vintages, the 1982 among them, were rich, ripe and ready young, and merchants in Britain and America were soon competing for the little there was. When winemakers in Saint-Émilion began in the 1990s to make tiny quantities of dense, new oaked wine in sheds and garages, writers called them garagistes, and Le Pin was named as their forerunner. The estate stayed small and never sought a rank: Pomerol has no classification, and Le Pin has made its name without one. In 2011 the family opened a new cellar beside the old house. It stands for the opulent side of Pomerol, the wine to pour when a guest wants pleasure young rather than in twenty years.

others.name: Vieux Château Certan
others.note: The neighbouring estate of the wider Thienpont family since 1924, made apart from Le Pin; a different wine, not its second.

traps: Le Pin has no classification: Pomerol has never been ranked, so its fame rests on the wine alone.
Le Pin and Vieux Château Certan share a family name but are separate estates with separate wines.
Le Pin is Pomerol, not Saint-Émilion, though most of the garage wines it inspired were made in Saint-Émilion.

cards.front: Le Pin: where does the estate's name come from?
cards.back: A lone pine tree beside the small house on the plot the Thienpont family bought in 1979.

cards.front: What name did writers of the 1990s give the tiny, dense Right Bank wines that followed Le Pin's lead?
cards.back: Garage wines, made by garagistes, mostly in Saint-Émilion; Le Pin is named as their forerunner.

questions.q: A guest asks how Le Pin is raised to taste of mocha and cream. Which answer fits?
opts: Large old casks for three years
Concrete vats, with no oak at all
Clay amphorae buried in the cellar
questions.exp: Le Pin goes into new oak barrels for its malolactic fermentation and its ageing; large old casks and bare concrete would give none of that mocha and cream.

questions.q: In what year did a branch of the Thienpont family buy the small Pomerol plot that became Le Pin?
questions.exp: They bought it in 1979 and made the first vintage that autumn; 1924 is when the family bought Vieux Château Certan nearby.

wine.name: Château Cheval Blanc
wine.classification: Premier Grand Cru Classé A from 1955 until it withdrew in 2021
wine.grapes: Cabernet Franc and Merlot in near equal parts, the Cabernet Franc often a little ahead.
wine.sites: Gravel, sand and clay in the far north west of Saint-Émilion, hard against Pomerol and its estates L'Évangile and La Conseillante, on land carved from Figeac from 1832.
wine.making: Each parcel is fermented apart in a concrete vat sized to it, in the cellar that opened among the vines in 2011. The wine is then aged for about a year and a half in new oak barrels and bottled at the château.
wine.glass: Violet, red plum and raspberry over sweet tobacco, mint and cedar, with truffle as it ages; silky and perfumed, with fine, satin tannin and a long, fresh finish.
wine.ageing: Charming in its first years, it then closes and opens again after fifteen or so; the great vintages last half a century and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The appellation, the stricter of Saint-Émilion's two; it is not a rank in the classification.
The rank printed on vintages made before the estate left the classification in 2021.
Bottled at the estate rather than by a merchant in Libourne or Bordeaux.

records.table: Château Cheval Blanc is the Saint-Émilion estate on the Pomerol border where Cabernet Franc leads Merlot on gravel and clay. Expect violets, red plum and silken tannin, perfume before power; its 1947 is a vintage of history.
records.story: The land of Cheval Blanc was once part of Château Figeac, whose owners sold vineyard from 1832 onwards. Through a marriage of 1852 it passed to the Fourcaud-Laussac family, who built the estate and held it for almost a century and a half; its name came, the story goes, from an old coaching inn where travellers changed horses. Medals won at the great exhibitions of the later nineteenth century were printed on the label. The 1947, picked in a scorching autumn, came out so ripe and dense that it is a vintage of history, talked of for its weight as a wine almost like Port. When Saint-Émilion drew up its first classification in 1955, Cheval Blanc and Ausone were the two estates ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé A, a rank they held alone until 2012. In 1998 the family sold the estate to two businessmen, and in 2011 a new cellar of concrete vats, one for each parcel, opened among the vines. In 2021 Cheval Blanc and Ausone withdrew from the classification, objecting to criteria that weighed marketing and tourism beside the wine in the glass. When a guest doubts that Cabernet Franc can lead a great Right Bank wine, Cheval Blanc is the answer to pour.

others.name: Le Petit Cheval
others.note: The second wine, Cabernet Franc and Merlot from the same vineyard.

others.name: Cheval des Andes
others.note: A Malbec led red of Mendoza, made with Terrazas de los Andes since the 1999 vintage.

traps: Cheval Blanc and Figeac share gravel and a history but are separate estates: Cheval Blanc's land was carved from Figeac.
Cheval Blanc left the Saint-Émilion classification in 2021, so its later labels carry no rank, though older bottles print Premier Grand Cru Classé.
Cheval Blanc is Saint-Émilion, not Pomerol, though its vines run to the Pomerol border.

cards.front: Château Cheval Blanc: which grape leads its blend, unusually for the Right Bank?
cards.back: Cabernet Franc, in near equal parts with Merlot and often a little ahead of it.

cards.front: Which Saint-Émilion estate grew from land carved from Figeac from 1832, and made a wine of history in 1947?

questions.q: A guest asks why Château Cheval Blanc tastes more perfumed than most Saint-Émilion. Which reason fits?
opts: Cabernet Franc leads, on gravel beside Pomerol
Cabernet Sauvignon leads, on the limestone côte
Merlot alone, on a rise of blue clay
Long ageing in large old casks
questions.exp: Cheval Blanc's Cabernet Franc on gravel gives violets and silk; Merlot on blue clay is Pétrus, and the limestone côte below the town is Ausone's ground.

questions.q: In 2021 Château Cheval Blanc left the Saint-Émilion classification. Which estate withdrew with it that year?
questions.exp: Ausone withdrew with Cheval Blanc in 2021 and Angélus followed; Figeac and Pavie became the two A estates of 2022, and Pétrus, in Pomerol, was never classified.

wine.name: Château Ausone
wine.classification: Premier Grand Cru Classé A from 1955 until it withdrew in 2021
wine.grapes: Cabernet Franc and Merlot in about equal parts, the Cabernet Franc often the larger share.
wine.sites: A south and south east facing amphitheatre on the limestone côte directly below the town, thin clay over the rock, with cellars quarried into the limestone beneath the vines.
wine.making: Fermented parcel by parcel in wooden vats and aged in new oak barrels for well over a year in the cellars cut into the rock, where the cool, even air slows the wine, before it is bottled at the château.
wine.glass: Crushed stone, blood orange and red cherry over violet, black tea and clove, cool and tightly wound; firm, fine grained tannin, high acidity and a long, chalky finish.
wine.ageing: Austere and closed when young, it needs twenty years in a strong vintage and can go on for many decades after.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Named for the Latin poet Ausonius, whose villa, by local belief, stood on this slope.
The appellation on the label, which is not the same thing as a rank in the classification.
Bottled at the estate, in the cellars cut into the limestone.

records.table: Named for the Roman poet Ausonius, Château Ausone grows on the limestone slope beneath the town of Saint-Émilion. Cabernet Franc with Merlot, it is cool, stony and tightly wound, a wine for the long cellar.
records.story: Ausonius (about 310 to about 395), the Latin poet of Bordeaux and tutor to the future emperor Gratian, wrote of his own vineyards, and local belief long held that his villa stood on this slope below the town, and the estate carries his name. The vines grow on the limestone côte, and the cellars run back into old quarries in the rock that once gave Saint-Émilion its building stone. When Saint-Émilion drew up its first classification in 1955, Ausone and Cheval Blanc were the two estates ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé A, a pair that held that rank alone for more than half a century. For much of that time the estate was shared between two branches of the owning family, and a long dispute between them ended in the mid 1990s, when one branch took sole charge of vineyard and cellar. Ausone kept its A rank in 2012, when Angélus and Pavie were raised to join it, but in 2021 it withdrew from the classification together with Cheval Blanc. Ausone is the voice of the limestone: cool, slow and built for the cellar, the opposite pole to Cheval Blanc's gravel.

others.name: Chapelle d'Ausone
others.note: The second wine, Cabernet Franc and Merlot from the same slope.

traps: Ausone is limestone côte and Cheval Blanc is gravel beside Pomerol: the two A estates of 1955 differ in soil and in style.
Ausone, Cheval Blanc and Angélus all withdrew before the 2022 revision, so Ausone's later labels print no rank.

cards.front: Château Ausone: whose name does it carry, and why?
cards.back: The Latin poet Ausonius of Bordeaux; local belief held that his villa stood on the slope below Saint-Émilion.

cards.front: On what ground does Château Ausone grow, and where are its cellars?
cards.back: The limestone côte directly below the town, with cellars cut into old quarries in the rock.

questions.q: A guest wants a Saint-Émilion grown on the limestone côte below the town rather than on gravel. Which estate fits?
questions.exp: Ausone's slope is limestone directly below the town; Cheval Blanc and Figeac grow on the gravel by Pomerol, and Le Pin is in Pomerol itself.

questions.q: Saint-Émilion's first classification, of 1955, placed two estates alone in its A rank. Which two?
questions.exp: Ausone and Cheval Blanc held the A rank alone until 2012, when Angélus and Pavie joined; Figeac and Pavie are the A estates of 2022, and Pomerol is never classified.

wine.name: Château Figeac
wine.classification: Premier Grand Cru Classé A in the 2022 Saint-Émilion classification
wine.grapes: Roughly a third each of Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Merlot, a share of Cabernet Sauvignon rare on the Right Bank.
wine.sites: Three low rises of deep gravel in the north west of Saint-Émilion, beside Cheval Blanc and the Pomerol border; the gravel warms quickly and ripens both Cabernets.
wine.making: Each parcel is picked and fermented apart, the Merlot first and the two Cabernets later, and the wine is aged for well over a year in new oak barrels before it is bottled at the château.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant leaf, cedar and graphite over red cherry, tobacco and a little mint, cooler and more structured than most Saint-Émilion; firm, fine tannin, fresh acidity and a long, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Reserved in youth, it opens after ten to fifteen years, and the strong vintages hold for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two and an old one off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The rank on the label; in 2022 Figeac was placed in its upper group, A.
The appellation, a stricter tier than plain Saint-Émilion and separate from the classification.

records.table: With about a third of Cabernet Sauvignon on gravel beside Cheval Blanc, Château Figeac tastes closer to the Médoc than its neighbours do: blackcurrant leaf, cedar and graphite. In 2022 it was raised to Premier Grand Cru Classé A.
records.story: In the eighteenth century Figeac reached across much of the north west of Saint-Émilion, on gravel where, the story goes, a Gallo-Roman family whose name it carries had a villa in the second century. In the nineteenth century its owners sold off land, among it, from 1832, the parcels that became Cheval Blanc. In 1892 the estate was bought by the family of Thierry Manoncourt (1917 to 2010), who took charge of it in 1947 after training as an agronomist. He kept and widened the plantings of Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc on the warm gravel, so that Figeac grew into the Right Bank's Cabernet estate, closer in taste to the Médoc than to its Merlot neighbours. In 1955 it was ranked Premier Grand Cru Classé in Saint-Émilion's first classification, in the group below Ausone and Cheval Blanc, and it stayed in that group through every revision for more than sixty years. In 2022, with Ausone, Cheval Blanc and Angélus gone from the list, Figeac was promoted to A beside Pavie. Offer it to a guest who loves Pauillac: three grapes in near equal parts, cedar before plum.

others.name: Petit-Figeac
others.note: The second wine, made in Figeac's cellar from the same three grapes.

traps: Figeac and Cheval Blanc share gravel and a history but are different estates: Cheval Blanc's land was carved from Figeac.
Figeac's blend carries about a third of Cabernet Sauvignon, so do not sell it as a Merlot wine.
Figeac was raised to A only in 2022, when Pavie, A since 2012, was the one other estate in the rank.

cards.front: Château Figeac: what sets its blend apart on the Right Bank?
cards.back: Roughly a third each of Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Merlot, an unusual share of Cabernet Sauvignon for Saint-Émilion.

cards.front: Which Saint-Émilion estate was promoted to Premier Grand Cru Classé A in 2022, alongside Pavie?

questions.q: A guest who drinks Pauillac wants a Saint-Émilion in a similar vein. Why does Château Figeac suit?
opts: About a third of its blend is Cabernet Sauvignon
It is all Merlot from a rise of blue clay
It grows on the limestone côte below the town
It is aged for years in concrete vats
questions.exp: Figeac's gravel carries about a third of Cabernet Sauvignon, giving cedar and graphite; blue clay Merlot is Pétrus, and the côte below the town is Ausone.

questions.q: Château Figeac once covered far more ground. Which neighbour grew from land carved from it from 1832?
questions.exp: Figeac's owners sold the vineyard that became Cheval Blanc from 1832; Ausone and Pavie lie on the limestone côte on the other side of the town.
